We performed a GWAS to identify potential associations between common variants and GCase activity in both cohorts separately, followed by a meta-analysis. We looked at the genomic inflation factors and QQ plots of each analysis to test for systematic bias and found them to be acceptable (Columbia lambda = 0.99, PPMI lambda = 1.04, Supplementary Fig. 1). The strongest associated locus in Columbia was in the GBA1 locus, as expected (Fig. 1A). This signal is driven by N370S (rs76763715, beta =  - 4.21, se = 0.35, p = 4.55e - 31), which is in linkage disequilibrium (LD) with the lead SNP in the locus (rs745550122, beta =  - 4.46, se = 0.35, p = 6.61e - 34, R2 = 0.78, D' = 0.91). A second signal can be seen in chromosome 17 in the GAA locus, with the strongest associated variants comprising a high-LD region (Supplementary Fig. 2) and the lead SNP having a negative direction of effect (beta =  - 0.96, se = 0.17, p = 7.55e - 9). Applying conditional and joint analyses revealed no secondary independent associations in either signal. We performed the same analysis in cases and controls separately to assess if there were any notable differences in associations between the two disease groups (Supplementary Fig. 3). The same GBA1 N370S peak is observed in both analyses with varied strengths of association (cases, b = - 4.18, se = 0.46, p = 9.16e - 19; controls, b = - 4.07, se = 0.56, p = 4.92e - 12), and no other genome-wide significant loci were observed. Notably, we do not see the GAA locus association in either analysis, which is due to a lack of power from the decrease in cohort size considering that the top variants in both analyses are in linkage disequilibrium with the same direction of effect (cases, rs9899138, b = - 0.86, se = 0.2, p = 3.19e - 05; controls, rs9905685, b = - 1.22, se = 0.3, p = 6.96e - 05; R2 = 0.72, D' = 0.91). The GBA1 signal was replicated in the PPMI cohort, with N370S once again driving the association (Fig. 1B, beta =  - 5.05, se = 0.76, p = 1.25e - 10). The GAA locus does surpass nominal significance in PPMI, although the lead SNP is different and has an opposite direction of effect compared to the lead SNP from Columbia (Table 2). The meta-analysis likewise showed associations in the GBA1 and GAA loci, but did not result in any additional associations (Fig. 1C). The GBA1 variants T369M (rs75548401) and E326 K (rs2230288) were associated with GCase activity, although the only association passing GWAS significance was T369M in the meta-analysis (Table 3). Both variants had similar effect sizes, directions, and p-values across both analyses, and patients who carried these mutations had similar GCase activity means to control carriers except for E326 K where patients show a decrease in activity in both cohorts (Supplementary Table 2). We also repeated these analyses with the inclusion of GCase outliers and found the results to be highly similar, with the GBA1 signals increasing in strength (N370S, beta =  - 4.62, se = 0.31, p = 6.95e - 50; T369M, beta =  - 3.66, se = 0.53, p = 5.04e - 12; E326 K, beta =  - 1.4, se = 0.41, p = 0.00071) and the GAA signal remaining mostly the same (rs9899138, beta =  - 0.99, se = 0.16, p = 1.37e - 08, Supplementary Fig. 4).

Interestingly, analysis in the Columbia cohort without adjusting for acid alpha-glucosidase activity eliminates any association from the GAA locus (Fig. 2A). Adding adjustments for common PD-relevant GBA1 variants N370S, E326K, and T369M results in both the GBA1 and GAA peaks dropping below GWAS-level significance (Fig. 2B). To better understand if these outcomes could be due to an interaction between the acid alpha-glucosidase and GCase enzymes, we constructed an interaction plot of enzyme activities by genotype of the top GAA SNP that was common in both cohorts (Fig. 2B). The genotype of the lead SNP in the GAA locus (17:78,061,141:T:G) appears to impact the interaction of GCase and acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme activities in Columbia, with correlations becoming progressively weaker in an additive manner with the addition of the T allele (Fig. 3). This trend is not as clear in controls, which could be due to the lower number of samples in this group. The effect is also not apparent in PPMI, reflective of the lack of association in this cohort. To further investigate the presence of an interaction, both an ANOVA and a linear regression using an interaction term were performed. The ANOVA used the absolute difference between GCase and acid alpha-glucosidase activity, which did significantly vary by the genotype status of the lead GAA variant (df = 2, sum Sq = 130, mean Sq = 64.75, F = 13.62, p = 1.52e - 06). The linear regression was performed using the same covariates as the previous analysis, with the addition of a GAA*GCase interaction term. The results indicated that the T/T genotype status was significant (beta =  - 0.25, se = 0.13, p = 0.048), supporting the presence of an interaction effect between GAA genotype status, acid alpha-glucosidase activity, and GCase activity. Notably, all enzymes in this model had a significant effect on GCase activity (GAA, beta = 0.63, se = 0.068, p = 2e - 16; ASM, beta =  - 0.1, se = 0.025, p = 2.78e - 05; GALC, beta = 0.12, se = 0.057, p = 0.037; GLA, beta = 0.32, se = 0.067, p = 2.56e - 06). An analysis of mediation provided evidence that acid alpha-glucosidase activity levels significantly mediate the relationship between GAA genotype and GCase activity (beta = 1.05, se = 0.12, p < 0.0001).

To examine if the GAA locus has any role in PD, we investigated the association of this region with PD risk and various measurements of progression using GWAS summary statistics from previous studies. We identified 26 variants nominally associated in the GWAS of PD risk, four with age at onset, five with UPDRS III scores, 79 with MoCA scores, and six with MMSE scores (Supplementary Table 1), although no variants passed Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. There were no GAA locus variants even nominally associated in the GWASs of motor, cognitive, and composite progression. Of the associated variants, eight variants from the GWAS of PD risk, two from the GWAS of age at onset, 33 from the GWAS of MoCA scores, and one from the GWAS of MMSE scores were also nominally associated with GCase activity in the present meta-analysis.

We investigated PD-related variants nominated from the largest PD GWAS to date to determine if any were associated with GCase activity in our cohorts (Nalls et al., 2019). There were 17 loci below nominal significance in the main GWAS for Columbia, seven in the GWAS for PPMI, and 14 in the meta-analysis (Table 4). Of these, only N370S (rs76763715) and rs35749011 (in strong LD with E326K) in the GBA1 locus, as well as rs13117519 in the ANK2 locus passed multiple testing correction in the meta-analysis. For our case and control stratified analyses, in addition to the GBA1 N370S signal, two PD-risk loci in SNCA became significantly associated with GCase activity in PD cases after applying multiple testing correction (rs356203, beta = 0.53, se = 0.17, p = 0.0015; rs356182, beta = 0.55, se = 0.17, p = 0.0017). When repeating the analysis with the inclusion of GCase outliers, we find the GBA1 E326K (rs35749011, beta =  - 2.29, se =  - 0.66, p = 0.001) and ANK2 (rs13117519, beta = 0.43, se = 0.14, p = 0.0011) loci to no longer be significant after Bonferroni correction. We then attempted to replicate previously reported associations in TMEM175 and LRRK2 with GCase activity by investigating these loci in a simplified meta-analysis using only age, sex, disease status, 10 PCs, and PD-relevant GBA1 SNPs including N370S, E326K, and T369M as covariates (Supplementary Fig. 4). There were three intronic variants in LRRK2 that passed nominal significance (rs116911375, beta =  - 1.7, se = 0.79, p = 0.03; rs191242488, beta =  - 1.041, se = 0.52, p = 0.044; 12:40,668,909:T:G, beta =  - 1.041, se = 0.52, p = 0.044), and no variants in TMEM175. No variants passed multiple testing corrections. The nominally significant variants do not appear to be in LD with G2019S or M1646T. Although these variants are not associated with GCase activity in our analysis, G2019S and M1646T do show a consistent positive direction of effect with what has been demonstrated in previous research (Table 5). The difference seen in our results compared to the nominal association of M1646T found in a very similar analysis in these cohorts performed by Sosero et al. is due to the removal of GCase outliers in our study. With the inclusion of outliers, we also see an association of this variant in our meta-analysis (b = 1.16, se = 0.38, p = 0.002, rs35303786).
Discussion

In the present GWAS, we identified variants in the GAA locus as potential modifiers of GCase activity, in addition to the known associations with GBA1 variants. GAA encodes acid alpha-glucosidase, and deficiency in this enzyme leads to the LSD Pompe disease. There is no known association between Pompe disease and PD, and the variants in the GAA locus are not associated with PD risk, age at onset, or various measures of progression. This is an important observation, since it may suggest that changes in GCase activity alone are insufficient to cause PD, or that the effects of GAA variants on GCase activity are too small to have a meaningful clinical effect. It was hypothesized that the mechanism underlying GBA1-associated PD is an imbalance or disturbance in the lysosomal glycosphingolipid metabolism pathway overall, rather than reduced GCase activity on its own. This is supported by the identification of other genes in this pathway that are associated with PD, such as SMPD1, GALC, ARSA, and ASAH1. Moreover, burden analyses of LSD genes have implicated this pathway in both European and Chinese populations. Previous work has also demonstrated that lysosomal enzymes are highly correlated, especially for GCase, acid alpha-glucosidase, and alpha galactosidase A, which is encoded by GLA. Taken into consideration with the interaction effect observed in the present study, there seems to be mounting evidence in favor of this hypothesis. The mechanism behind the interaction of GCase and acid alpha-glucosidase is still unknown. The products of GCase are lipids and glucose, while acid alpha-glucosidase hydrolyzes glycogen into glucose. Our observation of genotype-dependent correlation between GCase and acid alpha-glucosidase activities may therefore indicate that the GAA locus variants associated with GCase activity could maintain equilibrium in this pathway, as they affect both GCase and alpha-glucosidase activities. Overall, our results support that the association between GAA and GCase activity is complex, with additional genetic, enzymatic, and functional studies being required to determine the presently unknown mechanism behind it.

We further examined the association between known PD-associated loci and GCase activity. As to be expected, we found three PD variants in the GBA1 locus to be associated with GCase activity. We also found an additional association with the ANK2 locus. Phosphorylation in the ANK2 region has been proposed to play a role in PD neurodegeneration through the inhibition of organelle autophagy, but its connection to GCase activity is not clear from the current literature and will need further research. There are also multiple notable associations with ties to GCase activity that may have only failed multiple testing corrections due to sample size. One such locus is GALC, encoding the enzyme galactosylceramidase which, similar to GCase, breaks down large sphingolipids into lipids and ceramide. The association of GALC variants with GCase activity may suggest that a disturbance in lysosomal metabolism could be a causal mechanism in PD, which is also supported by a previous research that found galactosylceramide and GCase to be correlated. We also found nominal associations with multiple SNCA variants, complementing previous associations found between levels of alpha synuclein aggregates and Gcase activity. A third interesting locus that fell just shy of the multiple testing correction thresholds was FYN. This gene encodes a kinase that has been shown to phosphorylate alpha-synuclein, which is a key step towards its aggregation into Lewy bodies. We did not replicate previously reported associations with LRRK2 or TMEM175 variants, which are likely due to additional adjustments in our study and the removal of GCase outliers compared to previous studies. Studies in larger cohorts will be required to confirm the associations of these PD loci.

This study has several limitations. The first limitation is a lack of statistical power. Our discovery and replication analyses utilized the largest cohorts with enzyme activity measurements that were available at the time of performing the study and allowed us to complete the first GWAS of GCase activity. This enabled us to discover common variants with moderate effect sizes, such as the lead SNP of the GAA locus (rs9899138, beta =  - 0.99, MAF = 0.28) or rarer variants with large effect sizes, such as GBA1 N370S (rs76763715, beta =  - 4.21, MAF = 0.038). However, we are lacking in power to detect variants of smaller effect sizes and rarer allele frequencies, and thus are likely missing more modulators of GCase activity yet to be uncovered. Considering this is an exploratory analysis, we believe the methodology should be replicated in a larger, well-powered cohort when data is available. A second limitation is our inability to assess rare pathogenic GBA1 mutations, such as L444P, in our analysis of GCase activity. These variants were not present in our imputed genotype dataset and thus could not be analyzed, but could still exert significant effects on GCase activity. Studying these in future research will be important for understanding the relationship between GBA1 mutations and GCase. Another limitation is the use of only individuals of European and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, as there was insufficient data to carry out the study in other populations. Next, our study had minor differences in age and notable differences in sex, particularly in the Columbia cohort, between cases and controls. Both age and sex were adjusted for in all analyses to account for these differences. An additional limitation is the method of enzyme measurement used. Lysosomal activity was measured using dried blood spots, the methodology for which has been thoroughly tested and optimized. However, this method is not guaranteed to capture the true enzyme activity within a functioning lysosomal environment. These results will be strengthened if replicated in future studies that use lysosomal-specific methods of enzyme activity, in cells more representative of disease pathogenesis. Next, we were not able to adequately adjust for disease subtypes or severity in our analyses due to the data available for each cohort. This is a limitation of this study and similar studies that do not take these factors into account, as disease severity could have an effect on the results. Lastly, again due to the limitation of data available, we are undoubtedly missing adjustments for the influence of potentially influential confounding variables. We are also limited in how many confounding variables we can include in our analyses as our sample size increases the risk of overfitting.

In conclusion, we found a novel potential association in the GAA locus associated with GCase activity, which may represent an interaction effect between GCase and acid alpha-glucosidase and could be indicative of a homeostatic relationship between lysosomal enzymes. We also support previously suggested connections of multiple PD-related genes with GCase activity, such as GALC and SNCA, as well as identifying a novel potential association with ANK2. These findings could be significant for improving our understanding of how GCase deficiency is related to overall lysosomal dysfunction and how GCase functions in relation to other lysosomal enzymes. Additionally, associated loci can be taken into account in future research and clinical trials to help control for genetic influences on GCase activity. Due to the novelty of our results and lack of confident association in our replication cohort, further genetic and functional research will be required to validate our findings.

passages.text: Impact of ER stress and the unfolded protein response on Fabry disease
Summary

Fabry disease (FD) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic missense and nonsense variants in the alpha-galactosidase A (GLA) gene, leading to absent or reduced enzyme activity. The resulting lysosomal accumulation of the substrate globotriaosylceramide leads to progressive renal failure, cardiomyopathy with (malignant) cardiac arrhythmias and progressive heart failure as well as recurrent strokes, which significantly limits the life expectancy of patients affected with FD. There is increasing evidence that pathogenic GLA missense variants as well as formally benign GLA variants can cause retention in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), resulting in ER stress, which in turn triggers an unfolded protein response (UPR) leading to cellular dysregulation including inflammation, irreversible cell damage, and apoptosis.

This review aims to provide an update on the pathogenetic significance of ER stress and UPR in FD, current treatment options, including pharmaceutical and chemical chaperones, and an outlook on current research and future treatment options in FD.
Search strategy and selection criteria

Data for this narrative review were identified through comprehensive searches in PubMed, MEDLINE, https://clinicaltrials.gov/, and Web of Science. The search terms used included combinations of keywords related to Fabry disease, lysosomal storage disease, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and chaperones. Specific search terms included: "Fabry disease" OR "LSD" OR "ER stress" OR "UPR" OR "molecular chaperones" OR "4-PBA" OR "ambroxol" OR "chemical chaperones" OR "Gaucher disease" OR "MPS" OR "cystic fibrosis" OR "ER-associated protein degradation" OR "trehalose" OR "AGALopathy".

Articles published in English from 1983 to 2025 were included. The search was limited to peer-reviewed articles, and reviews. The reference lists of the selected articles were also manually screened to identify additional relevant studies.
1.Relevance: The study must be directly related to ER stress, UPR, and the potential treatment with a focus on Fabry disease or lysosomal storage diseases.
2.Quality: The study must be methodologically sound, with clear descriptions of the methods, results, and conclusions.
3.Originality: The study must present original research or comprehensive reviews that provide new insights into the field.
Selected studies were individually examined to determine their eligibility for inclusion in the review. Each article was meticulously evaluated based on the following criteria:
Articles that did not meet these criteria were excluded from the review. This selection process ensured a comprehensive and focused overview of ER stress, UPR, and Fabry disease.
Introduction

The maintenance of protein homoeostasis is crucial for the function and survival of all living cells. Newly synthesised proteins in the ER undergo chaperone-assisted folding to acquire their appropriate tertiary structure, before they can translocate to their subcellular targets. Protein folding is a highly error-prone process and up to 30% of all newly synthesised proteins are misfolded. This frequency increases if cells are exposed to stress, toxic components or if the synthesised protein is mutated. Misfolded proteins are often non-functional, can aggregate and become trapped in subcellular organelles and are therefore toxic to cells. As a consequence, high levels of misfolded proteins trigger a cellular response known as ER stress and contribute to the pathogenesis of many diseases, including type 2 diabetes and neurodegenerative disorders. Thus, pathogenic missense variants can not only lead to a loss of function, but can also trigger ER stress, modulating and aggravating a disease. Fabry disease (FD) is a rare lysosomal storage disorder, belonging to the sphingolipidoses. FD is characterised by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-galactosidase A (AGAL/GLA) resulting in an impaired degradation of the substrate globotriaosylceramide (Gb3). The progressive cellular Gb3 accumulation leads to the activation of proinflammatory and profibrotic signalling pathways, causing a multisystemic disease with vital organ damage. To date, there are >900 different GLA variants including missense mutations, leading to misfolded AGAL proteins that can also induce ER stress. While pathogenic nonsense variants generally result in early termination of translation and thus an absent protein, most missense GLA variants lead to an unstable and misfolded protein with reduced AGAL activities within affected cells. These variants can be divided into 5 categories according to their phenotypic expression: "pathogenic", "probably pathogenic", "unclear significance", "probably benign", and "benign". Classic FD is best exemplified by males with truncated or missense GLA variants who have no AGAL enzyme activity, increased plasma globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3) levels and intracellular Gb3 inclusions. These patients typically show first symptoms in early childhood and develop cardiac, kidney, and neurologic complications in the 3rd or 4th decade of life. Male patients with a late-onset phenotype have missense GLA variants, showing a moderately decreased AGAL activity (2-20% of normal) and a modest increase in plasma lyso-Gb3. In comparison to the phenotype of classic FD, the late-onset phenotype occurs later in life and is often limited to cardiac or kidney disease. For patients with a genetic variant of unclear significance, there is currently insufficient data to characterise them as either disease causing or as benign.

However, some patients with certain AGAL variants show clinical manifestations suggesting FD in the differential diagnosis. For example, neuropathic pain, which typically occurs in patients with FD with absent or low intracellular enzymatic AGAL activity. As these patients have normal or only slightly reduced AGAL enzymatic activity and no or only minor cellular Gb3 inclusions, FD can be excluded as a diagnosis.

A major effector could be the involvement of ER stress and the unfolded protein response (UPR), which may contribute to the observed pathogenesis of certain variants. It is generally assumed that misfolded proteins will not pass the protein quality control mechanism within the ER, resulting in a premature degradation before reaching the lysosomes. Therefore, it can be hypothesised that certain missense AGAL variants can lead to relevant ER stress and activation of the UPR, followed by cellular pathogenic processes, independent of residual AGAL enzymatic activity. This hypothesis is supported by the data on overexpression of mutated AGAL in cell culture demonstrating ER retention and subsequent UPR for certain variants.

The aim of this narrative review is to provide an update on the pathogenic significance of ER stress and UPR in FD, current treatment options including pharmaceutical and chemical chaperones, and an outlook on current research and future treatment options in FD.
ER stress and the three UPR pathways

The adaptive unfolded protein response (UPR) pathway. Following endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, three major UPR pathways can be activated. a) After activation, ATF6 passes from the ER into the Golgi apparatus, where it is cleaved by proteases. This produces an active cytosolic ATF6 fragment (ATF6alpha). This fragment migrates into the nucleus, binds to ATF6-responsive elements and activates the transcription of UPR target genes that are involved in the homoeostasis of ER protein folding, cell physiology, and protein secretion. In addition, unfolded or misfolded proteins that accumulate in the ER lumen can be degraded by the proteasome via proteasome-based ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD), which is regulated by the ATF6-mediated and/or IRE1alpha-X-box-binding protein 1 (XBP1)-mediated UPR branches. b) After dimerisation and phosphorylation, phosphorylated IRE1alpha splices cytosolic XBP1 mRNA, which encodes a potent transcription factor that activates the expression of UPR target genes involved in ER proteostasis and cell pathophysiology. IRE1alpha-RNase can also cleave ER-associated mRNAs or non-coding functional RNAs, leading to their degradation by regulated IRE1-dependent decay (RIDD), which modulates protein folding, cell metabolism, inflammation, and inflammasome signalling pathways. The cytosolic domain of IRE1alpha may also serve as a scaffold for the recruitment of adaptor proteins such as members of the tumour necrosis factor receptor-associated factor (TRAF) family, thus activating inflammatory responses under non-canonical ER stress conditions. c) After dimerisation and phosphorylation, PERK phosphorylates eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 subunit-alpha (eIF2alpha), thereby reducing the overall frequency of mRNA translation initiation. However, selective mRNAs, such as ATF4 mRNA, are preferentially translated in the presence of phosphorylated eIF2alpha. Upon translocation to the nucleus, ATF4 also activates transcription of UPR target genes encoding factors involved in amino acid biosynthesis, antioxidant response, autophagy, and apoptosis.

As the major site of protein biosynthesis and folding, the ER is capable of sensing and responding to the accumulation of misfolded proteins, a condition generally known as ER stress. A distinction must be made between physiological and pathological ER stress. While the ER physiologically controls protein quality, excessive ER stress, e.g., due to an excessive amount of misfolded protein, can contribute to pathological ER stress, triggering diseases. The complex cellular response to ER stress, also known as the UPR, is mediated by three ER-resident transmembrane proteins, which are introduced in Fig. 1 and described within the following section.
ATF6-mediated UPR signalling

Schematic organisation and overview of endoplasmic reticulum-associated protein degradation (ERAD). An E3 ubiquitin-ligase complex in the ER membrane coordinates the different ERAD steps beginning with the recognition of a misfolded protein (red). Proteins will be recognised on either side (ER lumen or cytosolic) or within the ER membrane. After recognition, misfolded proteins in the lumen and membrane are retrotranslocated to the cytosolic side of the ER membrane, facilitated by the membrane domains of ubiquitin-ligase complex components. After reaching the cytosolic side of the ER membrane, substrates are ubiquitinated by ubiquitin ligase E2. The cytosolic Cdc48/p97 complex binds to ubiquitinated proteins, facilitating the last steps of retrotranslocation by extracting the protein out of the ER membrane. Finally, cytoplasmic proteins direct the newly polyubiquitinated protein to proteasomes for degradation.

Activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6) acts as an ER stress sensor, which functions as an ER-membrane-bound transcription factor. Upon recognition of unfolded/misfolded proteins by the ER luminal domain of ATF6, the full-length protein translocates from the ER to the Golgi apparatus (Fig. 1a). There it is cleaved by proteases into several fragments, including the active cytosolic ATF6alpha, which migrates into the nucleus and induces the expression of UPR target genes. The resulting chaperones and enzymes such as BiP, ERp57, and PDIA6 play an important role in protein folding and secretion as well as ER/Golgi biosynthesis, enhancing the secretory capacity of these organelles. Other upregulated proteins such as GRp94 promote the proteasome-based ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD) to facilitate the degradation of misfolded proteins and maintain ER homoeostasis (Fig. 2).
IRE1-mediated UPR signalling

Inositol-requiring enzyme 1alpha (IRE1alpha) is an ER-transmembrane protein with dual enzymatic activity as a kinase and an endoribonuclease (RNase). Upon ER stress IRE1alpha oligomerizes and undergoes autophosphorylation, enabling it to splice an intron from the mRNA of the transcription factor X-box-binding protein 1 (XBP1) (Fig. 1b). This splicing event results in the translation of its active form XBP1s, which translocates into the nucleus and increases the expression of genes such as MDG1/ERdj4, IL-6, and EDEM1, which are involved in the translocation, folding and secretion of ER proteins, inflammation, ER and Golgi biosynthesis and the degradation of misfolded proteins. Prolonged ER stress can lead to regulated IRE1-dependent decay (RIDD), which describes the cleavage of mRNAs or precursor microRNAs (miRNAs) by IRE1alpha, resulting in their degradation (Fig. 1b). This process could reduce mRNA abundance and the associated protein folding load in the ER, but also shifts cellular signalling towards apoptosis since miRNAs, which normally repress pro-apoptotic genes, are depleted. In addition, members of the tumour necrosis factor receptor-associated factor (TRAF) family can associate with the cytosolic domain of IRE1alpha and subsequently activate NFkappaB-mediated inflammation, autophagy, and stress responses (Fig. 1b).
PERK-mediated UPR signalling

Protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK) is a sensor for ER stress, which dimerises and trans-phosphorylates in response to the accumulation of unfolded/misfolded proteins (Fig. 1c). The cytosolic kinase domain phosphorylates the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 subunit-alpha (eIF2alpha) leading to a temporary attenuation of protein synthesis. This mechanism prevents the influx of newly synthesised proteins into the ER and consequently reduces its protein folding-mediated burden. Additionally, eIF2alpha-P signalling upregulates a set of proteins, including the activation transcription factor 4 (ATF4) in turn promoting the expression of genes such as CHOP or GADD34, being involved in redox homoeostasis, amino acid metabolism, antioxidative responses, ER protein synthesis, and apoptosis. In order to restore protein synthesis after ER stress resolution, ATF4 also contributes to a negative feedback loop dephosphorylating eIF2alpha-P.
ERAD activation and function

The ER-associated degradation (ERAD) is a mechanism leading to the clearance of unfolded and misfolded proteins from the ER. The removal and subsequent degradation of these proteins helps to prevent an accumulation of misfolded proteins during ER stress, resulting in less UPR. Thus, cells with dysfunctional ERAD show a continuous UPR activation. However, the activation of ERAD can also have negative consequences for affected cells. An example has been demonstrated for the DeltaF508 variant of cystic fibrosis conductance regulator (CFTR (DeltaF508)), a variant expressed in most patients with inherited cystic fibrosis. Although the variant results in a generally fully functional protein, it leads to a recognition by ERAD and a premature degradation causing the disease. In principle, misfolded proteins are targeted for ERAD by utilising features such as prolonged association with endogenous chaperones, exposed hydrophobic regions or a specific N-linked oligosaccharide structure to generate so-called degrons.

While soluble proteins in the ER lumen are usually retrotranslocated through the HRD1-E3 complex, integral membrane proteins are processed via ERAD pathways and sent to the cytosolic side of the ER (Fig. 2). This step is mediated by the membrane domains of the E3 ubiquitin-ligase complex. Once exposed to the cytosolic side of the ER membrane, proteins are ubiquitinated by the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2 ligase). Subsequently, the cytosolic Cdc48/p97 complex binds to ubiquitinated proteins and mediates their extraction out of the ER membrane, followed by the deliverance to the cytosolic proteasome for final degradation (Fig. 2).
Differences between nonsense and missense variants in Fabry disease

Loss of function variants (including nonsense mutations, splice site mutations, and deletions or insertions) within the GLA gene lead to a lack of endogenous AGAL activity due to premature termination of protein synthesis causing FD. In male patients with FD, this usually results in a "classic" FD phenotype with an early onset of typical FD symptoms and manifestations, such as gastrointestinal symptoms, neuropathic pain, hypohidrosis, angiokeratomas, tinnitus, and cornea verticillata. These patients suffer from progressive multi-organ involvement during adolescence, affecting the kidneys, the heart, and the central nervous system. Additionally, they show lysosomal Gb3 inclusions in almost all cells/tissues of the body and high levels of lyso-Gb3 in plasma. The biochemical effects of missense variants within the GLA gene are much more diverse. Depending on their localisation within the protein, they can lead to null mutations with little to no AGAL activity (e.g., mutations within the catalytic centre) or to variants with only moderately reduced enzymatic AGAL activity. While the former variants generally also lead to a "classical" FD phenotype, variants leading to residual AGAL enzymatic activity may result in a "late-onset" phenotype characterised by a later onset of the first symptoms/manifestations within the third or fourth decade of life and mainly limited to cardiac manifestations with only mild involvement of other organs and only moderately elevated plasma lyso-Gb3 levels. The best characterised variant leading to a "late-onset" phenotype especially of the heart (cardiac insufficiency, left ventricular hypertrophy, and arrhythmias) the p.N215S variant, is also called "cardiac" variant. The change in the amino acid at position 215 leads to a lack of glycosylation, which is required for correct intracellular transport to the lysosomes via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor. As a result, the majority of the mutant protein is retained in the ER, leading to decreased AGAL activities in lysosomes and additionally to ER stress and UPR. Currently, it is not known which AGAL variants in FD trigger pathologic ER stress and UPR and thus could contribute to the observed clinical phenotype. Current data suggest that ER stress may contribute significantly to the pathogenesis of FD, but the direct effects cannot be sufficiently distinguished from the secondary consequences of lysosomal dysfunction. Additionally, according to current knowledge, the present phenotype ("classic" versus "late-onset") cannot be used to conclude the pathophysiological mechanism of substrate accumulation (Gb3) or ER stress.
Potential ER stress and UPR in Fabry disease

Alterations in ER proteostasis and UPR signalling were identified as being involved in a variety of human diseases, such as cancer, neurodegeneration, and metabolic diseases. For a detailed review, refer to Hetz et al. 2020. In the following part, the potential involvement of the UPR as a diseases mediator in FD, a member of lysosomal storage disorders (LSDs), will be discussed. In principle, the lack of lysosomal AGAL activity is responsible for classic FD. However, this does not fully explain the clinical findings for non-classic or late-onset phenotypes and variants in FD, in which affected patients present with FD-like manifestations despite (significant) intracellular AGAL activity and absent or little lysosomal Gb3 inclusions. While nonsense variants usually result in premature termination of translation and subsequent degradation, this does not usually apply to missense variants, where point mutations merely lead to an exchange of amino acids.

In detail, AGAL is synthesised in the ER, post-translationally modified with mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) and translocated to the lysosome via the secretory pathway. Specific GLA variants can affect the synthesis, processing, and stability of AGAL in different ways. The misfolding of some AGAL variants and their accelerated degradation by ERAD lead - comparable to nonsense variants - to a lack of lysosomal enzyme and thus to FD. In contrast, chronic induction of the UPR, as in the case of continuous production of a mutant protein, may lead to cell death or activation of inflammation and could, therefore, also play a pathological role in patients with AGAL variants, similar to other diseases. However, this has not yet been sufficiently investigated for AGAL and results are controversial. In a previous study, the expression level of some ER stress markers in peripheral blood mononuclear cells of patients with FD and control subjects was analysed and no clear differences were found. Unfortunately, no information on the underlying AGAL variants was provided in this study, and since it can be assumed that the variants in the analysed patient cohort were heterogeneous including missense and nonsense variants carriers, the outcome is not surprising. By contrast, an ER retention followed by an activation of the UPR was demonstrated in a fly model expressing two AGAL variants (p.A156V and p.A285D). So far, most studies analysing the location of different AGAL variants were based on artificial heterologous expression in various cell culture models including wild type COS-1, COS-7 or HEK293 or nowadays AGAL-deficient HEK293T cells. The heterologous expression of p.R112C, p.C172G, and p.G411D in COS-7 cells resulted in a retention within the ER, while the benign variant p.D313Y translocated to the lysosomes, properly. Furthermore, the heterologous overexpression of 8 AGAL missense variants (p.R100T, p.D165V, p.D231N, p.N263S, p.A288D, p.M296I, p.R301Q, p.G360D) in AGAL-deficient HEK293 cells revealed that variants with residual activity (p.D231N, p.N263S, p.M296I, p.R301Q, p.G360D) showed decreased lysosomal localisation and only partial retention in the ER compared to wild type, while missense variants without residual activity (p.R100T, p.D165V, p.A288D) were fully retained in the ER. While only cells expressing p.D165V, p.A288D, and p.R100T showed an increased BiP expression, the two variants p.G360D and p.R301Q showed an activation of the ATF6 UPR branch, too. A comparable study of the controversially discussed and probably benign variant p.S126G showed similar results, in that overexpression in wild type COS-7 cells resulted in an ER retention and activation of the PERK UPR branch. The so-called cardiac variant p.N215S was analysed in the same work, showing no retention within the ER, which was explained by a rapid degradation due to ubiquitination. Interestingly, an increased AGAL secretion (measurable within cellular supernatants) was not considered. If the authors idea would be considered further, it would also mean that cells (and thus patients) expressing this variant should not exhibit (any) AGAL activity. However, for the p.N215S variant it was repeatedly demonstrated that affected cells and patients present with decreased but measurable AGAL activities. Unfortunately, the authors neither discuss their contradictory result nor place it in the context of the literature. A recent case study analysed the effect of the missense variant p.N5D, which is localised within the signal peptide of AGAL, formed by the first 31 amino acids. Overexpression of the mutant protein resulted in an increased expression of BiP, morphologic ER injuries and intra-lysosomal inclusions, while PBMCs of the affected patients showed an increased inflammation signalling. The most comprehensive study so far concerning AGAL misprocessing-induced ER stress and UPR was published by Zivna and colleagues. In this study, the intracellular distribution of several missense AGAL variants in patient-derived fibroblasts as well as stable or transiently transfected HEK293 cells was analysed. Interestingly, pathogenic variants associated with classic and non-classic FD (p.R112H, p.A135V, p.L294X, p.R301Q, and p.R342Q) localised to lysosomes and demonstrated characteristic biochemical abnormalities and histopathologic findings in kidney biopsies. By contrast, missense AGAL variants associated either with non-classic, later-onset FD (p.A97V, p.Q279E, and p.M296I) or variants of unknown significance (p.L394P, p.E66Q, p.R118C, p.A143T, p.R252T, and p.D313Y) localised to the ER. Despite some limitations, this work provides additional fundamental insights into FD and UPR, proposing an interesting new concept of "AGALopathy". The AGALopathy concept is explained by the pathogenic effects of misfolded AGAL variants due to abnormal intracellular retention of these AGAL variants resulting in ER dysfunction with pathogenic UPR. AGALopathy is thus not FD, which is based on an enzyme deficiency resulting in intracellular Gb3 accumulation. Thus, AGALopathy cannot be successfully treated with ERT. Future studies are now warranted addressing this concept adequately.

Overview of the intracellular alpha-galactosidase A trafficking and the potential impact of missense variants leading to reduced lysosomal enzymatic activities, enzyme retention within the ER or Golgi apparatus. AGAL: alpha-galactosidase A, CGN: cis-Golgi network, ER: endoplasmic reticulum, GA: Golgi apparatus, Gb3: globotriaosylceramide, TGN: trans-Golgi network.

Most of the current data need to be interpreted carefully, since in some studies, no AGAL activities for the analysed variants were provided and most importantly, the experimental setup was mainly based on an artificial transient overexpression of AGAL constructs partially with c-terminal HA or FLAG tags, driven by strong expression promoters lacking appropriate transfection controls. Tags at the c-terminal end of AGAL may have a general impact on protein folding (tertiary and dimerisation). In addition, the high protein expression may lead to incorrect localisation due to a lack of glycosylation of the expressed protein. Of note, the latter might also occur in vivo with gene therapies. The high expression may lead to an accumulation within the ER. The resulting ER stress is followed by an increased secretion of not yet proper glycosylated proteins limiting gene therapy efficacy. Similar to the absent cross-correction in females with FD, the target protein cannot be internalised by other cells via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor due to the absent M6P residue. Nevertheless, despite limitations described, the following model for the effect of individual missense AGAL variants on ER stress and UPR might be proposed (Fig. 3). Some variants such as p.N215S might mainly be stuck within the ER. While some molecules might finally reach the lysosomes and degrade Gb3, the main proportion triggers UPR and ERAD.

Globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3) is the deacylated form of Gb3. Due to the lack of the ceramide, lyso-Gb3 is more hydrophilic and thus more soluble (in plasma) than Gb3 and, therefore, considered to be a better biomarker for disease burden and progression in FD patients than plasma Gb3. Lyso-Gb3 is also involved in the pathology of FD, as it triggers cellular inflammatory processes in a concentration-dependent manner. Since lyso-glycosphingolipids are often associated with neurodegenerative disorders, a recent experimental study analysed the toxic effect of lyso-Gb3 in an immortalised neuronal cell line (SH-SY5Y). The authors identified that under lyso-Gb3 concentrations mimicking classical FD, lyso-Gb3 specifically binds and causes ubiquitination of cellular chaperones such as HSP90, HSP60, and the T-complex protein Ring Complex (TRiC). Hence, it is conceivable that high lyso-Gb3 concentrations could additionally influence and worsen AGAL variant-dependent ER stress and UPR. Thus, an (early) reduction of plasma lyso-Gb3 under FD-specific therapy might reduce the described ER stress and UPR, which needs to be demonstrated in future studies.
Pharmacological targeting of ER stress by chaperones

Overview of the different chaperone classes. a) Molecular chaperones facilitate the correct folding of unfolded proteins so that they can leave the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by vesicular transport via COPII vesicles. Pharmacological chaperones bind specific proteins and facilitate their correct folding, e.g., by binding to the active centre of an enzyme like migalastat. b) Chemical chaperones can be divided into osmolytic and hydrophobic components. Osmolytes act directly on unfolded proteins to stabilise their conformation, preventing protein-protein interactions and leading to a more stable state due to their hydration effect. Hydrophobic components can reduce the aggregation of unfolded proteins, increase the expression of molecular chaperones and promote the secretion of unfolded proteins via COPII vesicles. c) 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) can act as a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, modulating gene expression to promote molecular chaperone synthesis. Additionally, 4-PBA can reduce the accuracy of quality control mechanisms regulating the translocation of proteins from the ER by interacting with the COPII coat components. By inhibiting an element of the ER quality control machinery, 4-PBA enables the retained misfolded proteins to escape the ER, lowering ER stress by relieving the burden of accumulated proteins.

Treatment strategies that enhance the activity or expression of endogenous molecular chaperones can alleviate ER stress by improving protein folding capacity and reducing the load of misfolded proteins. Further treatment strategies include pharmacological chaperones, which specifically bind their target proteins, causing them to refold or stabilise, leading to a reduction of ER stress. Another approach is the indirect reduction of ER stress by eliminating the misfolded proteins and restoring cellular homoeostasis. This can be achieved by an increased secretion of misfolded proteins or normalising autophagy, which is also often disturbed due to increased ER stress. Chaperones can be divided into three groups, including molecular, pharmacological, and chemical chaperones (Fig. 4). Most molecular chaperones are stress proteins or heat shock proteins (Hsps), since their biosynthesis is triggered under stress conditions (e.g., heat shock or oxidative stress), which structurally destabilise many of the cellular proteins. The members of the different groups of chaperones are named according to their molecular weight: e.g., Hsp40s, Hsp60s, Hsp70s, Hsp90s, Hsp100s. In addition to their fundamental role in the de novo folding of proteins, chaperones are involved in various aspects of proteome maintenance, including the assembly of macromolecular complexes, protein transport and degradation, and the dissociation and refolding of protein aggregates. Furthermore, Hsps play an important role in regulating the cell metabolism. Under ER stress conditions, expression and synthesis of molecular chaperones will be upregulated.
Overview of chemical and pharmaceutical chaperones used for the treatment of various diseases and lysosomal storage disorders.

Pharmacological chaperones can be defined as a separate group (although they are chemical compounds), since they act as reversible and competitive inhibitors of their target proteins, causing them to refold or stabilise. Most pharmacological chaperones are small molecules and very specific. To avoid a continuous inhibition of their targets, they are used in low concentrations. A well-known example of a disease treatable with pharmacological chaperones is cystic fibrosis. Screening approaches identified compounds promoting a proper folding and trafficking of the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) resulting in either stand alone or combination treatments with lumacaftor (VX-809) and ivacaftor (VX-770) to correct the folding and increase the gating activity of CFTR (Table 1). One pharmacological chaperone is also approved for the treatment of FD (migalastat; 123 mg orally every other day; Amicus Therapeutics). The small molecule 1-deoxy-galactonojirimycin (DGJ) is a competitive inhibitor of AGAL. By reversibly binding to the enzymes' catalytic centre, DGJ/migalastat stabilises and increases endogenous AGAL activity of amenable variants, by supporting a correct folding within the ER, followed by a proper trafficking to the lysosomes. Due to the mechanism of action, only patients with missense variants that have been tested positive for amenability in in vitro tests can be treated with migalastat (GLP-HEK assay). Healthcare professionals can check the individual GLA variants for amenability online [https://www.galafoldamenabilitytable.com/hcp/]. Although migalastat is approved for the treatment of FD since 2016, to the best of our knowledge, no appropriate studies were published elucidating the effect of migalastat on ER stress in migalastat-treated patients, adequately. However, a pre-clinical study based on a fly model for FD assessed the impact of migalastat on UPR and ERAD mediated by the missense variants p.A156V and p.A285D. While an expression of both mutant proteins within the fly's dopaminergic cells led to UPR activation resulting in cell death, treatment with migalastat alleviated the UPR.

While migalastat reversibly binds to the active site of AGAL, tafamidis (Vyndaqel), another pharmaceutical chaperone, selectively binds to transthyretin (a transport protein), inhibiting the dissociation of tetramers into monomers. Tafamidis is indicated for the treatment of hereditary and wild-type transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy. The therapy with tafamidis reduces mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalisations and slows the progression of peripheral neurologic impairment. Pharmaceutical chaperones can also be used to stabilise and prolong the plasma half-life of enzyme replacement therapies. As an example, in Pompe disease, miglustat is used as a stabiliser for cipaglucosidase alfa during infusion. One hour before the start of the infusion, the patient takes 65 mg miglustat orally (Table 1). Interestingly a comparable approach for FD was performed 10 years ago (NCT01196871). In a clinical trial, Warnock and colleagues combined ERT with migalastat to increase the infused enzymes' half-life in patients with FD. Following co-administration of migalastat and agalsidase, AGAL activity in plasma was significantly increased 1.2- to 5.1-fold compared to agalsidase administration alone. Similar increases of AGAL activities in skin and PBMC were observed, too, suggesting that the co-administration of migalastat 2 h before infusions with either agalsidase alfa or agalsidase beta can lead to greater systemic exposure and tissue levels of active AGAL in patients with FD. In terms of the additional costs, this treatment approach would even be acceptable, since in addition to ERT, only one capsule of migalastat would be added to each infusion. Unfortunately, this treatment concept was not followed further, probably due to different marketing companies.

Chemical chaperones do not necessarily counteract all misfolded proteins directly. Since many of them require a very high intracellular concentration to be effective, their use as potential therapeutic agents is limited.

Chemical chaperones can be categorised into two groups (Fig. 4b). Chemical osmolyte chaperones are generally effective at millimolar concentrations. Currently it is assumed that they form a protective barrier that limits or prevents protein-protein interactions (and thus aggregation), as it has been demonstrated for trehalose. They can also induce proper folding by mediating a hydration shell, which also increases solubility. For example, trehalose depletes the disordered protein surface water by trehalose-water structure formation, resulting in a decreased disorder and aggregation and increased activity. Trehalose has also been shown to indirectly reduce ER stress in neurodegenerative disease models by stimulating the degradation of misfolded proteins through the activation of autophagy. The increased autophagy is probably due to an activation of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), which could be mediated by increased beclin 1 expression.

Certain other osmolytic chemical chaperones were found and appear to act in multiple cellular compartments. For example, the small amino acid glycine is able to protect organisms in high-salt environments, polyols such as glycerol protect against extreme temperatures and dehydration, and methyl-amines including trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) enable some cell types to deal with high concentrations of urea.

In contrast to osmolytes, hydrophobic chaperones can directly bind to hydrophobic residues acting as detergents. As an example, tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) decreases toxic protein aggregates in cells and reduces ER stress. Another important hydrophobic chaperone, which is used (experimentally) for the treatment of various diseases and in basic research is 4-phenylbutyrate (4-PBA; Table 1). 4-PBA acts in different ways, by inhibiting histone deacetylases (HDAC), and therefore promoting the transcription of different targets (Fig. 4c). In addition, 4-PBA shows chaperone activity by inhibiting misfolded protein aggregation. Furthermore, 4-PBA increases trafficking and secretion of mutant proteins normally retained in the ER by inhibiting the formation of COPII vesicles (Fig. 4c). The use of 4-PBA for a potential clinical application in animal models was analysed for many diseases, including rare diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), cystic fibrosis, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, but also in ischaemia, epilepsy and cartilage diseases, such as chondrodysplasias and osteoarthritis (Table 1). However, most of the clinical studies for 4-PBA were terminated due to poor outcomes and worsening of symptoms.

Another promising hydrophobic chaperone is ambroxol (known as an expectorant for respiratory diseases with thick mucus), especially for the treatment of Gaucher disease (GD) and beta-glucocerebrosidase (GBA; GCase)-associated Parkinson disease. GD is caused by more than 860 known GBA1 variant alleles, many of them translated into a misfolded enzyme with reduced or absent activity, resulting in a lysosomal storage disorder. In addition, following ERAD, the proteasome is overwhelmed resulting in an aggregation and accumulation of misfolded GCase molecules triggering ER stress and UPR. Ambroxol is described as a pharmacological chaperone for mutant GCase in high doses, mediating the correct folding and functional recovery.

As a consequence, recent detailed systematic reviews conclude that overall high-dose ambroxol shows promising effects in managing neurological manifestations and thus could be considered as a treatment for Gaucher disease in future. However, the dosages used in the studies analysed varied widely and ranged from ~75 to 1300 mg per day. Hence, further clinical trials are essential for elucidating dosage-response relationships and refining treatment outcomes and strategies for Gaucher disease. Ambroxol was also reported to increase enzyme activity of certain AGAL and acid alpha-glucosidase variants, either alone or in combination with migalastat or deoxynojirimycin, respectively, in cell culture experiments, suggesting their potential use as enzyme activity enhancer for the treatment of FD and Pompe disease.

It is important to note that it is not yet clear whether ER stress-mediated UPR activation plays a direct role in the manifestation of phenotypes in these diseases. Future studies need to elucidate the pathophysiological link between ER stress, UPR and disease phenotypes. In conclusion, the chaperones described above could act in different ways in FD or AGALopathy. The chemical chaperones such as 4-PBA and ambroxol could correct the misfolding of AGAL missense variants in a similar way to the other diseases. On the one hand, they could increase the endogenous enzymatic AGAL activity and, on the other hand, reduce the resulting ER stress. Furthermore, it is conceivable that the secretion of misfolded AGAL could be induced or, as demonstrated for trehalose, autophagy might be induced, which could also reduce ER stress and the UPR. An increase in the half-life and stabilisation of ERT using migalastat has already been shown clinically, but has not yet been implemented in clinical practice. A synergistic effect of ambroxol on the enzymatic activity of migalastat-responsive variants of AGAL has also been described in cell culture experiments.
Outstanding questions

There is currently a clear need for more information and research to elucidate the potential involvement of ER stress and the UPR in the pathogenesis of FD. It needs to be analysed whether and how missense variants contribute to the pathogenesis of FD. In this respect, it should be clarified whether the observed symptoms and manifestations are due to reduced lysosomal AGAL activity and/or whether excessive ER stress characterises the clinical picture. Studies should address whether and how already approved chaperone therapies such as migalastat can reduce existing ER stress in addition to increasing endogenous AGAL activity. As further possible therapeutic options, chemical chaperones already approved for the treatment of other diseases should be investigated regarding their efficacy in FD.

Due to the large number of known variants in the GLA gene and the associated different effects on folding, trafficking, and intracellular activity, patient- and respective variant-specific approaches should be chosen for clarification. Thus, since phenotypes in FD are heterogeneous, studies to analyse ER stress, UPR and effects of new chaperones in FD have to be well designed. As potential biomarkers the UPR-mediated mRNA expression of BiP, XBP1s, and ATF4 could be analysed. Cohorts that are aimed to be analysed and compared to (healthy) controls should be strictly separated into patients with pathogenic missense and nonsense GLA variants. It will also be very useful to evaluate patients with genetic variants of unknown significance or benign GLA variants separately. Proper tools and experimental setups to analyse AGAL variant-specific ER stress should include patient-specific cells to analyse endogenous AGAL expression, rather than relying solely on artificial overexpression models in cell culture. If the use of overexpression constructs cannot be avoided, the constructs should ideally have no or only small tags and the expression should not be driven by too strong promoters. Standard transfection controls to elucidate transfection efficacies, which have to be carried out for such experiments, are indispensable. These controls should include either co-transfections with reporter genes (ideally with the same plasmid) or PCR-based quantification of the transfected plasmids.

passages.text: Assessing osteopenia and osteoporosis with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry studies in Fabry disease
Background

Fabry disease (FD) is a rare multi-systemic lysosomal storage disease that affects the heart and kidneys most significantly. An underappreciated manifestation of FD is reduced bone mineral density. Currently, there are no specific guidelines for routine bone density assessments, and treatment of osteoporosis and osteopenia in FD.
Materials and methods

To ascertain the frequency of low bone mineral density in FD we studied dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scans obtained as part of routine care from a cohort of 25 individuals followed at the University of California:Irvine Medical Center for the period 2008-2023. The most recent BMD results for the lumbar spine and femoral neck were collected from 12 males and 13 females to examine the prevalence of low bone mineral density. The lowest Z- and/or T-scores of either lumbar spine or femoral neck were selected for analysis. Demographic factors, disease and ERT status, and other laboratory values were collected concurrently (within +- 9 months) with DXA scan results and were analyzed with Z- and T-scores to assess for correlations. In our cohort the mean age was 51 years (median 56 years, range 18-77 years). The Z-scores for all participants and T-scores from postmenopausal women and men >= 50-year-old were analyzed and correlated with various measures including disease duration, BMI, renal function (measured by eGFR), plasma GL3, Lyso-GL3, calcium, vitamin D, and alkaline phosphatase levels. These parameters were concurrent with DXA scan results.
Results

The average Z-score for all the participants was -1.2 +- 1.3 (range -4.6 to 1.6). Twenty-four percent of all participants (n = 6) had significantly low Z-scores <= -2.0. To identify the frequency of subjects with osteopenia, defined as T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 and osteoporosis defined as T-score < -2.5, T-scores were analyzed in postmenopausal women (n = 8) and men 50 years and older (n = 7). Of these 15 individuals, average T-score was -2.2 +- 1.3 (range -5.4 to 0.3), and 86.7% (n = 13) had abnormal results (osteopenia and osteoporosis), 53.3% (n = 8) had osteoporosis and 33.3% (n = 5) had osteoporosis. We found a significant difference in Z-scores between male (-1.98 +- 1.33) and female patients (-.45 +- 0.82) t (23) = 3.487 (p =  < 0.001). We did not find any differences in z-scores between different ethnic backgrounds. There was a strong negative correlation between Z-scores and Lyso-GL3 levels [r (15) = -.72, p = .001] and a moderate positive correlation between Z-scores and body mass index (BMI) [r (23) = .43, p = .033]. No correlation was found between Z-scores and calcium levels. There is a strong negative correlation between T-scores and Lyso-GL3 levels [r (8) = -.86, p = .001] and a negative correlation between T-scores and participants' ages at the time of DXA [r (13) = -.57, p = 0.028]. There is a positive correlation between T- scores and calcium levels [r (12) = .58, p = 0.030]. No significant correlation was observed between T-scores and BMI. There was no correlation between Z or T- scores and disease duration, duration of ERT use, renal function (measured by eGFR), GL3, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase levels, or their use of vitamin D or concomitant antiepileptic medications.
Conclusion

The findings of this cohort highlight the high prevalence of low bone mineral density in FD and correlations of low Z and T- scores with elevated levels of Lyso-GL3, and low calcium levels. We did not find correlations with renal function, and vitamin D levels. We discuss etiology, prevention, and treatment strategies for osteopenia/osteoporosis in Fabry disease.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s13023-025-03601-x.
Introduction

Fabry disease (FD) is a rare X-linked lysosomal storage disease caused by pathogenic variants in the GLA gene that lead to deficiency of the a-galactosidase A (AGAL-A) enzyme, which in turn leads to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (GL-3) and globotriaosylphingosine (Lyso-GL3) in the lysosomes. Fabry disease is found among all ethnic, racial, and demographic groups. The incidence of classic FD has been projected form 1:50,000 to 1:117,000 males while late-onset FD is more common and affects about 1 in every 1,500 to 4,000 males. The reported prevalence of FD detected through newborn screening per births is 1:7057 in Japan, 1:3100 in Italy, 1:3859 in Austria, and 1:1250 in Taiwan. In the US, the reported incidence is 1:8454 in Illinois (including the p.A143T variant), and 1:2913 in Missouri. Individuals with FD are affected in a multi-systemic manner and require multi-disciplinary specialist care. The heart and kidneys are affected most significantly and can lead to organ failure. Other common symptoms of FD include, but are not limited to, peripheral neuropathy, corneal whorls, angiokeratomas, hearing loss, and hypohidrosis. First reported in 2005, twenty hemizygous male patients with Fabry disease have been observed to have an increased risk of low bone mineral density (BMD), an underappreciated association. In a cross-sectional study in 53 patients in Denmark at a mean age of 40 years with untreated FD, 46% (n = 24) of the patients had femoral neck osteopenia and 27% (n = 14) had osteopenia of the lumbar spine. Another study in France retrospectively observed the musculoskeletal manifestations in a cohort of 14 Fabry patients who had undergone bone absorptiometry. Fifty seven percent (n = 8) had abnormal results. Of the three males with osteoporosis, two had vertebral fractures. Osteoporosis was diagnosed in three females while two females had osteopenia.

Possible causes of osteoporosis and osteopenia include reduced calcium absorption, low vitamin D levels, renal failure, secondary hyperparathyroidism, steroid therapy, and the use of antiepileptic agents for pain control. However, none of which have been clearly linked to FD as being the primary explanation. Currently, there are no specific guidelines for routine bone density assessment and treatment of osteoporosis and osteopenia as part of FD standard of care. Moreover, despite being a subject of interest to FD researchers, there is paucity of related awareness information for patients in prominent rare disease and patient support sites. The aims of this retrospective study are to assess the prevalence of osteoporosis and osteopenia in FD patients; identify potential correlations between low BMD and demographic or clinical factors including disease duration, duration of ERT use, BMI, renal function (measured by eGFR), creatinine, GL3, Lyso-GL3, calcium, vitamin D, and alkaline phosphatase levels; and to provide insight on the effect of FD treatment on bone density.
Methods
Summary of demographics and clinical parameters of 25 patients with Fabry disease
